catalog_quote: Luvian has only three vowels, /a/, /i/, and /u/, in contrasting short and long varieties. While there are some underlying long vowels, most phonetic length is due to synchronic rules which lengthen underlying short vowels under the accent: contrast sentence-initial conjunction pā < /pá/ versus enclitic -pa < /-pa/, or adverb ānnan "under" < /ánnan/ versus annān pātanza "under the feet" < /annán/ with accent shift in a prepositional phrase (see Melchert 1994a:247 for further discussion). ... Certain facts about the placement of the accent may be inferred from the prehistoric and synchronic rules cited in the preceding two paragraphs, but the evidence is limited, and the risk of circularity of argument is high.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: is a 64-page image-only scan (the PDF's metadata); the 300-dpi render scanned/ carries the running header "580 The Cambridge Encyclopedia of the World's Ancient Languages" (cropped and viewed), so PDF p. 31 = book p. 580 as stated. I viewed scanned/ myself: sec. 3.2 Vowels reads exactly as quoted, including the diacritics the scanned drops (pā < /pá/ vs -pa < /-pa/; ānnan "under" < /ánnan/ vs annān pātanza "under the feet" < /annán/; "see Melchert 1994a:247"), and the second paragraph "Certain facts about the placement of the accent may be inferred from the prehistoric and synchronic rules cited in the preceding two paragraphs, but the evidence is limited, and the risk of circu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The source gives no placement rule: the accent of this extinct language is known only indirectly, through accent-conditioned vowel lengthening reflected in cuneiform plene spellings (accented short vowels in open syllables and initial position lengthen; unaccented vowels, e.g. enclitics, do not) and through prehistoric sound changes. Where inferable it is a free/mobile inherited (Indo-European-type) accent that can differ between homophonous forms (/pá/ vs. enclitic /-pa/) and shift within a phrase (/ánnan/ vs. /annán/ in annān pātanza), i.e. not fixed to any syllable. Yakubovich 2013:115 says the same in Russian: the synchronic nature of Luwian stress is unclear; only stressed word forms vs. enclitics can be told apart.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shift onto the final syllable of the adverb in a prepositional phrase (ānnan 'under' /ánnan/ vs. annān pātanza 'under the feet' /annán/); enclitics are unaccented (-pa vs. pā). Rieken 2017:24 adds that Čop's Rule presupposes first-syllable stress in mallī(t)- 'honey', while the place of stress in many lexemes remains uncertain (Rieken 2017:27; Yakubovich 2008:394 fn. 10 for the same caveat in Hittite).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent inferred from orthography (plene writing) of a dead language attested 16th-13th c. BCE; the word/phrase contrast is explicit (accent shift in a prepositional phrase). Melchert's phonology is stated to be based primarily on Cuneiform Luvian data, though the chapter covers both Cuneiform and Hieroglyphic Luvian.
new_statements.identity_note: Melchert 2004 covers 'Luvian' as one language written in two scripts and states (p. 579) that its phonological analysis is based primarily on Cuneiform Luvian data, so the accent statement applies to cune1239; Hieroglyphic Luwian is a separate Glottolog entry (Hieroglyphic Luwian, iso hlu; code not verified here). Yakubovich 2013 likewise treats Luwian as a whole, with the cuneiform corpus representing the Kizzuwatna ritual koine and 'Empire Luwian' words in Hittite texts. Rieken 2017 is specifically on Cuneiform Luwian.

sources.note: Sociolinguistic study, not a grammar. a full-text search for stress/accent/stress/plene: no Luwian stress-placement statement. Fn. 10 p. 394 (on Hittite): follows Melchert (1994: 133) in assuming lengthening of every stressed e but does not implement it 'in view of many lexemes with the uncertain place of stress'. Other 'Luvian accent' hits (pp. 452, 538) mean foreign accent in L2 Hittite.

sources.note: p. 115 sec. 5.1.0: 'Синхронный характер ударения в Л.я. неясен' (the synchronic nature of stress in Luwian is unclear); only fully-stressed word forms vs. enclitics can be distinguished. p. 113: plene spelling probably marks vowel length by analogy with Hittite, inconsistently; p. 109: initial plene <a> reflects a glottal stop, not stress or length.

sources.citation: Rieken, Elisabeth. 2017. Word-internal plene spelling with <i> and <e> in Cuneiform Luwian texts. Journal of Language Relationship 15(1-2): 19-30. DOI 10.31826/jlr-2017-151-206.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Summary p. 27 sec. 6: plene <i> in Luwian marks long /ī/ 'which arises from original or anaptyctic /i/ under the accent (attested in open syllables..)' plus contraction, monophthongization and syncope sources; p. 27 sec. 4: in unetymologized words 'nothing forbids us to assume that the position of the stress was on the plene written syllable, which would then be regularly lengthened'; p. 24: Čop's Rule implies first-syllable stress in mallī(t)- 'honey'. Treats accent as lexically inherited, with position often uncertain.

sources.note: Phonology section (preprint pp. 16-17) gives the consonant and vowel inventory (short and long /a i u o/, phonemic length contrast of limited scope) and says nothing about accent placement; the only accent mention is that clause-second clitics attach to the first accented word of the clause.

sources.citation: Melchert, H. Craig. 1993. Historical Phonology of Anatolian. Journal of Indo-European Studies 21(3-4): 237-257.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: sec. 6.5 (p. 249): Luvian lengthens all short vowels in accented open syllables and all accented short vowels in absolute initial position; sec. 9 Accent (pp. 254-255): no systematic description attempted; Anatolian accent has an element of stress as well as pitch; its position is mostly maintained from Common Anatolian. No placement rule for Luvian.
